meta.note: Keyframe poses for the stick figures. Joints are three-dimensional and drawn in code with Compose Canvas; no image files and no third-party animation assets, so everything here works offline and can ship in a public repo.
meta.coordinate_space: Every joint is [x, y, z], centred on the figure and roughly between minus a half and plus a half. x runs left to right, y runs up to down, so a larger y is lower. z runs away from the viewer to toward the viewer.
meta.camera: Each exercise names its own camera in degrees. Azimuth 0 looks straight down the z axis, so you see the x-y plane; azimuth 90 looks along the x axis instead. Elevation lifts the viewer above eye level. Because the poses are three-dimensional, changing the camera shows the same movement from a different angle rather than needing new poses.
meta.symmetry: mirror_z reflects the written-down arm and leg across z, for exercises laid out along x such as a push-up. mirror_x reflects across x, for exercises facing the camera such as a pull-up. none means the two sides genuinely differ and both are written out, as in a split squat.
meta.how_to_fix_a_pose: Move the numbers, not the drawing code. Keep the distance between two joints about the same across every pose of one exercise, or the limb will appear to stretch as it moves. A test fails if it does.
meta.review_status: push_up, pull_up and hollow_hold are the first three, built for approval before the other twelve.

body.note: Thicknesses for the solid figure. The joint centres in each pose are the skeleton; these turn it into a body. Shoulders and hips are placed out to each side of the neck and pelvis along the body's own left-right axis, so no pose has to write them down.
body.proportions: A torso is about half as wide as it is long, and a head is a little under half the torso's length. The first attempt made the torso as wide as it was long, which read as a slab and swallowed the head.

anatomy.note: The muscles are the body. Each form is a shaped mass riding on a bone: the ones an exercise works go amber, the rest stay mist, and together they make the figure's silhouette. Drawn in code, so no anatomical model is licensed or bundled.
anatomy.segments: torso runs from the shoulder line to the hip line. upper_arm is shoulder to elbow, forearm elbow to wrist, thigh hip to knee, shin knee to ankle.
anatomy.fields: from and to run along the segment. side is which way the mass sits, relative to the body. lift is how far out from the bone, as a multiple of the form's own radius. across shifts it sideways: on the torso in fractions of the half width, on a limb in fractions of its radius. mirror repeats it at the opposite across. Limb forms are always drawn on both limbs.
anatomy.not_really_muscles: Grip, Core, Balance and trunk and Shoulder stabilizers are functional descriptions rather than single muscles. Each is attached to the forms that do the work, and they are listed here so the choice is visible and can be corrected.
anatomy.fidelity: Smooth masses, not sculpted anatomy. There are no striations and the contours are approximations, which is why the cue card says the shading is schematic.

push_up.facing_note: Face down: y is positive downward, so a prone exercise faces straight at the floor.
push_up.camera_note: Turned twenty degrees off a straight side view so both arms and both legs are visible, and tilted slightly down so the floor reads as a floor.

variants.note: Feet elevated on a chair. push_up_feet_up already draws exactly this movement, so it is referenced rather than copied and cannot drift from it.

pull_up.facing_note: Hanging and facing the viewer, which is why this one is drawn almost straight on.
pull_up.camera_note: Almost straight on, because the arms spread sideways and that is the whole shape. A few degrees of turn keeps it from looking flat.

variants.note: Negatives or feet-assisted. The body makes the same shape, so the poses are unchanged; what differs is a chair under the toes to step up from, and a sequence that only lowers. Authoring new joint positions here would risk a stretched limb for no gain.

hollow_hold.facing_note: On your back, so the front of the body points at the ceiling.
hollow_hold.camera_note: Turned and tilted more than the push-up, because lying on your back is the hardest position to read from dead level.
hollow_hold.variants_note: The base pose is rung 3 of the ladder: arms overhead, legs straight. Rung 1, the tuck, is where most people start and needs its own drawing.

variants.note: Tuck hollow. The torso is unchanged; the knees fold toward the chest and the arms come down beside the hips. Every limb keeps the length it has in the base pose.
Arms by sides, legs straight. The base pose already has the legs straight; only the arms come down, to the same positions the tuck uses.
Legs lower while the back stays down. The torso and arms are the base pose; the legs swing nearer the floor, which is what makes it harder. Thigh, shin and foot keep their base lengths.

Hollow rocks. The hollow shape does not change; the whole body rocks about the hip. Both poses are the base rotated six degrees either way, and a rigid rotation about one point preserves every distance, so no limb can stretch here.

Feet elevated on a chair, 0.071 above the floor, the same lift push_up_feet_up uses. The whole leg and hip translate up by that amount; the hands then have to come back from x 0.190 to 0.120, because with the hips higher the torso and arm together can no longer span the old distance. That is what the movement really does: it tips toward a handstand.
Negatives or feet-assisted. Same shape, a chair under the toes, and a sequence that only lowers.

inverted_row.props_note: The bar is drawn as a chair so it gets uprights down to the floor. A bare horizontal line above a figure reads as nothing in particular.

variants.note: Knees bent, feet flat on the floor at y 0.300. The torso and arms are unchanged; only the legs fold. Knee positions were solved as a circle intersection from the hip and the planted ankle so the thigh and shin keep their base lengths (0.1426 and 0.1354).

Lying reverse crunch. The easiest rung is not a hanging exercise at all: you are on your back on the floor. That needs its own facing and symmetry, or every muscle highlight lands on the wrong side of a body that is no longer upright. Torso, arms and legs all keep their base lengths.
Straight-leg raise. The hang is unchanged; only the raised pose differs, with the legs straight out in front instead of the knees folded. The longer lever is the whole of what makes it harder.

bulgarian_split_squat.facing_note: Standing and facing along positive x, the direction the front foot points.
bulgarian_split_squat.symmetry_note: The legs genuinely differ: one forward on the floor, one behind on a chair.

single_leg_hip_thrust.facing_note: Shoulders on a bench and hips up, so the front of the body points at the ceiling.

variants.note: Both feet. The base figure has one leg in the air; here the raised leg is planted beside the other, mirrored in z. Every limb keeps the length it has in the base pose.

side_plank.facing_note: On your side, so the front of the body points at the viewer.
side_plank.stacking_note: The legs are stacked one above the other rather than side by side, because lying on your side turns the body's left-right axis vertical. That is what mirror_y means here: the shoulders and hips stack too, instead of sitting side by side and reading as lying face down with a propped arm. Both limbs are still written out, because a side plank's two sides genuinely differ.

variants.note: Bent-knee side plank. The torso line is unchanged; the bottom knee comes down to the floor at y 0.312 and both shins fold back behind, still stacked one above the other. Every limb keeps the length it has in the base pose.
Top leg raised. The bottom leg and the whole torso are the base pose; only the top leg lifts, its knee solved from the hip so the thigh keeps its 0.1377 length.

Both feet, flat on the floor. The standing leg is mirrored to the other side and the step prop goes. The rise is smaller than on a step, 0.022 against 0.060, because without an edge to drop the heel below there is less range to travel.

Single leg on a flat floor. The same leg does the work, but the foot is flat rather than on a step edge, so the heel cannot drop below the forefoot. The raised foot is flexed up to keep it clear of a floor it would otherwise pass through.
